editorial_contributions.text:
The eigenvalues of graphs, most often defined as the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix, have received much attention in 50's and 60's of the 20th century as a means of characterizing classes of graphs and for obtaining bounds on properties such as diameter, girth, chromatic number, connectivity, etc. The interest has since then shifted somewhat from the adjacency spectrum to the spectrum of the closely related graph Laplacian. In particular, Laplacian graph spectra are being investigated as a means of characterizing large ``small world networks'' and random graphs.

This book focuses on mostly geometric properties of the eigenvectors themselves. Chapter 1 provides necessarry definitions (matrix representations, landscapes, generalized graph Laplacians). In Chapter 2 results concerning Laplacians are summarized (Rayleigh quotient, basic properties of eigenfunctions, quasi-abelian Cayley graphs, Perron-Frobenius theorem). Chapters 3 and 4 deal with eigenfunctions and nodal domains (Courant's nodal domain theorem, algebraic connectivity, Fiedler vectors, Perron branches, Courant-Herrmann conjecture). In Chapter 5 various computational experiments are described (nodal domains and hyperplane arrangements, hillclimbing algorithm, etc.). Finally, Chapter 6 covers Faber-Krahn type inequalities (unweighted and semiregular trees, rearrangements and Dirichlet operators, perturbations).

editorial_contributions.text:
This book provides a concise introduction to spectral graph theory and its applications. It is essentially divided into two halves: the first half of the book sets the scene with background on graph theory and related fields to which spectral graph theory can be applied. The second half treats the theory of graph spectra and various applications of spectral graph theory.

In the first chapter, the reader is familiarised with basic notions of graph theory, and a few examples of special graphs are presented. The second chapter discusses graph invariants that can be studied using techniques of spectral graph theory: chromatic number, independence number, diameter and girth, and the isoperimetic number. The third chapter covers regular graphs, with a special focus on Cayley graphs. Thereafter, the book briefly leaves the realm of pure graph theory and covers finite fields, in particular squares in finite fields, and characters of finite abelian groups with an emphasis on characters of finite fields.

Starting with Chapter 7, the reader learns about spectral graph theory and its applications. First, eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix and Laplacian matrix are introduced, and a few basic properties and examples are presented. Next, the author discusses methods to compute eigenvalues of special classes of regular graphs, such as Cayley graphs and strongly regular graphs. Chapter 9 treats the largest eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix and the Laplacian matrix, in particular various bounds and extremal results involving these eigenvalues. In Chapter 10, the study is extended to all eigenvalues of a graph, again providing various bounds.

Chapter 11 exhibits spectral methods to study some of the purely graph-theoretical concepts that were covered in the early chapters. Specifically, one learns about spectral bounds for the chromatic number, the independence number, the isoperimetric constant and certain edge counts. The closing chapter covers further selected topics of spectral graph theory: the largest eigenvalue of \(C_4\)-free graphs, and eigenvalues of Erdős-Rényi graphs.

This book can be recommended as a textbook for a first course on spectral graph theory, suitable for advanced undergraduate students. Each chapter also contains a number of exercises whose solutions are given at the end of the book.

editorial_contributions.text: This rich and interesting paper deals with topics related to the chromatic difference sequence, a parameter simultaneously detailing the chromatic and independence properties of a graph: Let \(c\) be the chromatic number of \(G\), and \(n_i\) the maximum cardinality of an induced \(i\)-colourable subgraph of \(G\), for \(i=1,2,\dots,c\). Then the chromatic difference sequence of \(G\) is \(n_1,n_2-n_1,n_3-n_2,\dots,n_c-n_{c-1}\). Note that the first term, \(n_1\), is the independence number of \(G\), and that the sum of all terms in the sequence is \(n\), the number of vertices of \(G\). The normalized chromatic difference sequence, ncds, is obtained by dividing each term by \(n\). The ncds allows for a comparison between graphs of different sizes. For instance, if \(G\) admits a homomorphism (edge-preserving vertex mapping) to a vertex transitive \(H\), then the ncds of \(G\) dominates the ncds of \(H\), see \textit{M. O. Albertson} and \textit{K. L. Collins} [Discrete Math. 54, 127-132 (1985; Zbl 0572.05024)]. The first half of the paper deals with the ncds of product graphs. The Cartesian product of graphs \(G, H\) has vertices \(V(G) \times V(H)\) and edges \((g,h)(g',h')\) such that either \(g=g'\) and \(hh'\) is an edge of \(H\), or \(h=h'\) and \(gg'\) is an edge of \(G\). A graph \(G\) such that the ncds of \(G \times G\) is the same as that of \(G\) is called stable. All Cayley graphs of abelian groups are stable, including all circulant graphs [\textit{H. Zhou}, Discrete Math. 90, No. 3, 297-311 (1991; Zbl 0734.05046) and Discrete Appl. Math. 41, No. 3, 263-267 (1993; Zbl 0783.05051)]. The author proves that the first \(\omega\) terms of the ncds of a stable graph \(G\) must be equal (with common value \(n_1/n\)), where \(\omega\) is the clique number of \(G\). Moreover, if \(G\) is a stable graph of odd girth \(2k+1\), then the third term of its ncds is at least \(n_1/kn\) and \(n_1/n \leq k/(2k+1)\). This implies that a triangle free stable graph \(G\) with all degrees greater than \(3n/8\) has the independence ratio \(n_1/n\) equal to \(2/5\) (the lower bound follows from a result of \textit{R. Häggkvist} [Ann. Discrete Math. 13, 89-99 (1982; Zbl 0492.05047)], and, for \(k > 2\), if the stable graph \(G\) has odd girth at least \(2k+1\) and all degrees greater than \(n/(k+1)\), then its independence ratio is equal to \(k/(2k+1)\) (the lower bound follows from a result of \textit{M. O. Albertson, L. Chan} and \textit{R. Haas} [J. Graph Theory 17, No. 5, 581-588 (1993; Zbl 0781.05028)]). The second half deals with the ncds of circulant graphs. A circulant graph with symbol \(S\) has vertices \(0,1,\dots,n-1\) and edges \(ij\) such that \(| i-j| \) or \(n-| i-j| \) is in \(S\). All circulants with the same symbol \(S\), regardless of the number of vertices \(n\), are shown to have their independence ratio \(n_1/n\) bounded above by the independence ratio of an auxiliary graph \(U(S)\). This allows the author to derive detailed information on the limit of the independence ratio \(n_1/n\), as \(n \rightarrow \infty\), for a fixed symbol \(S\). The paper concludes with several conjectures and open problems.

editorial_contributions.text:
This book is a very good survey of graphs defined on rings. The authors have collected results on almost all types of graphs related to rings. The book consists of ten chapters and an exhaustive bibliography of 443 items. The approach of the authors is ``historical''. They have tried to cover as many topics as possible. Since proofs of most of the results are known, the same are omitted. However, detailed comments, examples and references are given.

\textbf{Chapter 1: Introduction.} In this chapter basics of algebra and graph theory are given. These make the reading of the book easy, even to a beginner. 

\textbf{Chapter 2: Distances in zero divisor graphs}: In this chapter some properties of zero divisor graph (denoted by \(\Gamma(R)\)) on a commutative rings \(R\) are given. In particular, some necessary and sufficient condition, when \(\Gamma(R)\) is finite, when \(\Gamma(R)\) is complete are given. Relationship among \(\Gamma(R)\) and the zero divisor graphs of polynomial ring over \(R\) and formal power series ring over \(R\) is discussed. Properties such as diameter, girth of \(\Gamma(R)\) and those of zero divisor graphs of direct product of rings are given. 

The authors have illustrated these properties by giving examples. Rings without identity and their zero divisor graphs are discussed. Examples are given to show the differences between \(\Gamma(R)\) of a commutative ring with identity and that of a commutative ring without identity. For example it is shown that \(K_{2,2}\) can only be realized as \(\Gamma(R)\) of a commutative ring \(R\) with identity and \(K_5\) can only be realized as \(\Gamma(R)\) of a commutative ring \(R\) without identity.

\textbf{Chapter 3: Properties of zero divisor graphs.} In this chapter the authors consider some more graph theoretical properties such as coloring, connectedness, bipartite nature, isomorphisms and automorphisms of zero divisor graphs of commutative rings. 

The authors consider the ring \(\mathbb{Z}_n\) and find chromatic number of \(\Gamma(\mathbb{Z}_n)\) for certain \(n\). It is shown that \(\Gamma(\mathbb{Z}_n)\) is perfect if and only if \(n = p^k\) for some prime \(p\) or \(n = p_1p_2\) for distinct primes \(p_1\), \(p_2\).

Edge coloring of \(\Gamma(R)\) is considered. The authors consider the question.

\textbf{Question.} If \(R\) and \(S\) are commutative rings, is \(\Gamma(R) \cong \Gamma(S)\) if and only if \(R \cong S\)? 

For finite reduced rings, this holds true. An example is given to show that the finite hypothesis is necessary.

Some properties of automorphisms and isomorphisms are discussed. The following questions are discussed.

\textbf{Question.} Are there only finitely many finite rings \(R\) for which \(\mathrm{Aut}(\Gamma(R))\) is solvable (respectively, abelian)?

The questions, when is \(\Gamma(R)\) complete, bipartite are discussed.

The zero divisor graph of Gaussian integers is discussed. The study of zero divisor graphs of certain quotient rings are considered. 

The questions such as when is \(\Gamma(R)\) complemented, uniquely complemented, Hamiltonian, Eulerian are discussed. 

\textbf{Chapter 4: Genus of zero divisor graphs.} Genus of zero divisor graphs is discussed. Planarity of the zero divisor graph of a commutative ring is discussed. The following result is considered. 

\textbf{Theorem.} If \(R\) is a commutative local ring of cardinality 32, that is not a field, then \(\Gamma(R)\) is not planar. 

Examples of planar graphs, which cannot be realized as \(\Gamma(R)\) for any commutative ring are discussed. Zero divisor graphs with genus one and two are considered.

An example is given to provide a lower bound for the genus of the zero divisor graphs of nonlocal rings. Noncommutative local rings with genus of the zero divisor graph 2 are characterized. It is shown that for an infinite commutative ring \(R\), the genus of \(\Gamma(R)\) is either \(0\) or \(\infty\). It is also shown that for every positive integer \(g\), there are only finitely many finite commutative rings of genus \(g\). 

\textbf{Chapter 5: Generalized zero divisor graphs.} Various types of generalizations of zero divisor graphs of commutative rings are considered, for example ideal based zero divisor graph. If \(I\) is an ideal of \(R\), in general, \(\Gamma_I(R)\) need not be isomorphic to \(\Gamma(S)\) for any commutative ring \(S\). Properties of \(\Gamma(R/I)\) are considered. In fact, it is shown that for \(n \geq 2\), there exists a commutative ring \(R\) with a nonzero ideal \(I\) such that \(K_n \cong \Gamma_I(R)\). Some properties of \(\Gamma_I(R)\) are proved. Primal ideal based and annihilating ideal based zero divisor graphs are considered. Properties of compressed zero divisor graphs and extended zero divisor graphs are given.

\textbf{Chapter 6: Zero divisor graph generalizations.} The concept of the zero divisor graph is generalized to various other structures such as noncommutative rings, commutative semigroups, lattices, posets etc. 

The concept of directed zero divisor graph of a noncommutative ring is studied. Some properties of these graphs such as diameter, connectedness diameter etc. are proved. Some examples of these graphs are given. Properties of directed graphs of the ring of \(n \times n\) matrices over \(R\) are considered. Directed zero divisor graphs of finite rings are considered. Zero divisor graphs of semigroups, commutative semirings are considered. These graphs have properties similar to zero divisor graphs of commutative rings. However, it is shown that in the case of commutative rings, the ideal based zero divisor graph has no cut vertex but there exists a semiring which has an ideal with respect to which the ideal based zero divisor graph has a cut vertex.

Graphs related to modules and multiplication modules are considered. The concept of domination in zero divisor graph is studied. 

\textbf{Chapter 7: Total graphs of commutative rings.} Let \(R\) be a commutative ring with identity. The total graph of \(R\), denoted by \(T(\Gamma(R))\) is the simple graph, with vertex set \(R\) and two distinct \(x, y \in R\) are adjacent if and only if \(x + y \in Z(R)\). Some properties of these graphs are given. Characterizations/ conditions are given for these graphs to be Eulerian or Hamiltonian. Results related to coloring, domination, connectivity, perfectness of these graphs are discussed. 

\textbf{Chapter 8: Graphs from total graphs.} Properties of total graphs without the zero element in the vertex set are considered. Zero divisor graphs and regular paths are considered. Complements of total graphs, generalized complements of total graphs, line graphs of total graphs and their properties are discussed. 

\textbf{Chapter 9: Generalized total graphs.} Ideal based generalized graphs, total graphs of multiplicatively closed sets, total graphs of multiplicatively prime sets of commutative rings are discussed. Total torsion element graphs of a module, total graph of of a module, of a semiring, identity summand graph of a semiring are studied. 

\textbf{Chapter 10: Other graphs associated with rings.} Various other graphs associated with commutative rings such as Cayley graphs, comaximal graphs, units graphs, cozero divisor graphs, Jacobson and intersection graphs, annihilator graphs, compressed annihilator graphs, congruence based graphs, element graphs, dot product graphs are discussed. The trace graph of rings of matrices, ideal based trace graphs of rings of matrices over commutative rings are considered. Graphs of noncommutative rings based on elements such as commuting graph, nilpotent and idempotent graphs, graphs of ideals, divisor graphs are also discussed.
